changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $i\in I$, put $q=q_i$ and let $T_{i,c,t}$ be the toral binomials of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]. Write $E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $E^{(a)}=E_i^{(a)}$, $F^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}$.

(i) **Divided-power multiplication.** For all $a,b\ge0$, $E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iE^{(a+b)}$ and $F^{(a)}F^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iF^{(a+b)}$ ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]).

(ii) **Toral recursion and commutation.** $T_{i,c,t}=\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-t+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+t-1}}{q_i^{t}-q_i^{-t}}T_{i,c,t-1}$ for $t\ge1$; the $T_{i,c,t}$ are Laurent polynomials in $K_i^{\pm1}$ and commute with each other and with all $K_h$; and $E_iT_{i,c,t}$, $F_iT_{i,c,t}$, $T_{i,c,t}E_i$, $T_{i,c,t}F_i$ lie in $U_A^0E_i$, $U_A^0F_i$, $E_iU_A^0$, $F_iU_A^0$ respectively, i.e. the toral factor can always be moved to the middle at the cost of a scalar $q$-power and a shift of the binomial index.

(iii) **Reordering identity.** For all $a,b\ge0$ and $\min(a,b)\ge t\ge0$,
$$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}=\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}F_i^{(b-t)}\,T_{i,\,2t-a-b,\,t}\,E_i^{(a-t)},$$
with all coefficients equal to toral quantum binomials of $U_A^0$; in particular $E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$ and $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(a)}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}F_i^{(a-t)}T_{i,2t-2a,t}E_i^{(a-t)}$. For $i\ne j$ the divided powers $E_i^{(a)}$ and $F_j^{(b)}$ commute with one another, and $E_i^{(a)}$ commutes with $E_j^{(b)}$, $F_i^{(a)}$ with $F_j^{(b)}$, up to the toral action.

(iv) **Triangular spanning.** Every element of $U_A$ is an $A$-linear combination of products $b_-\,u\,b_+$ with $b_-\in U_A^-$, $u\in U_A^0$ and $b_+\in U_A^+$; equivalently $U_A=U_A^-U_A^0U_A^+$ as an $A$-module (no independence is asserted here; it is [[thm-integral-triangular-decomposition-for-the-lusztig-form]]).

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $U_A$ be the Lusztig integral form of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], with its subalgebras $U_A^-,U_A^0,U_A^+$, and let $m:U_A^-\otimes_AU_A^0\otimes_AU_A^+\to U_A$ be the multiplication map $x_-\otimes x_0\otimes x_+\mapsto x_-x_0x_+$.

(i) $m$ is an isomorphism of $A$-modules. Equivalently, every element of $U_A$ has a unique expression as a finite sum of products $x_-x_0x_+$ with $x_\pm\in U_A^\pm$, $x_0\in U_A^0$, and the product families are independent.

(ii) $U_A^\pm$ is a free $A$-module, graded by root degree in $Q_+$; each root-graded piece $U_A^\pm[\pm\nu]$ is a finitely generated free $A$-module whose rank equals the classical $\mathrm{PBW}$ rank $\dim_{\mathbb Q}U(\mathfrak n^\pm)[\pm\nu]$ of [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]].

(iii) $U_A^0$ is a free $A$-module; a basis is obtained by lifting any homogeneous $A$-basis of the associated graded of the toral-degree filtration (the filtration by the highest power of $K$ occurring in a Laurent polynomial), and the toral generators $K_h$ ($h\in P^{\vee}$) and $T_{i,c,t}$ are homogeneous for it.

(iv) $U_A$ is a free $A$-module: for each root degree $\beta$ the multiplication isomorphism restricts to
$$U_A[\beta]\cong\bigoplus_{\alpha,\gamma\in Q_+,\,\alpha-\gamma=\beta}U_A^+[\alpha]\otimes_AU_A^0\otimes_AU_A^-[\gamma],$$
which is a direct sum of free $A$-modules; and $U_A$ is the direct sum of its root-graded pieces.

No independence of the simple-generator words is claimed: the halves are presented by the quantum Serre relations and their $A$-bases are not the divided-power words.
changed_native_views.current_statement: Assume AC only for the generic/classical PBW rank supplier. Over A=Z[q,q^-1], multiplication U_A^-⊗_A U_A^0⊗_A U_A^+→U_A is an isomorphism. The two divided-power halves are free A-modules with finite free root components of the classical PBW ranks. The unmodified torus has an A-basis K_c∏K_i^{delta_i}T_{i,0,t_i}, with delta_i=0 or1 and c representing Pvee/Σ Z(d_i h_i). Hence U_A is free, and the degree-beta component is ⊕_{alpha,gamma∈Q_+, alpha-gamma=beta} U_A^-[-gamma]⊗U_A^0⊗U_A^+[alpha]. Unique coefficients refer to products of chosen basis elements, not to arbitrary sums of simple tensors.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group and $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ its Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]], [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]); recall $q_i=q^{d_i}$, $K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$.

A $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$ is a **weight module** if
$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu,\qquad M_\mu=\{m\in M:K_hm=q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}m\ \text{for all }h\in P^{\vee}\},$$
where the eigenvalues are the elements $q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}\in\mathbb Q(q)$ for integral weights $\mu\in P=\mathrm{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ of [[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]; $M_\mu$ is the **weight space** of weight $\mu$ and $\mathrm{wt}(M)=\{\mu:M_\mu\ne0\}$ the **weight set**. Type-one modules are those admitting such a decomposition; the decomposition is unique when it exists, and the nonzero weight spaces are then linearly independent.

A weight module $M$ is **integrable** if in addition, for every $i\in I$, the operators $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent: for every $m\in M$ there are integers $N_E,N_F\ge1$ (depending on $i$ and $m$) with $E_i^{N_E}m=0=F_i^{N_F}m$.

Neither finite dimensionality of the weight spaces, nor boundedness of the weights, nor a uniform nilpotence exponent is required; the zero module is a weight module and integrable. The hypotheses "all weight spaces are finite-dimensional" and "the weight set is contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$" are used separately where they are needed ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]], [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]]). This is the quantum analogue of [[def-integrable-kac-moody-module]]; the $K_h$-eigenvalue convention and the integrality of the weights are the only structural differences. No choice principle occurs in this definition.
changed_native_views.current_statement: For the published Cartan datum with possibly nonperfect pairing, a P-graded type-one quantum weight module is a module equipped with a direct sum M=⊕_{mu∈P}M_mu such that K_h acts on M_mu by q^{<mu,h>}, E_iM_mu⊂M_{mu+alpha_i}, and F_iM_mu⊂M_{mu-alpha_i}. These are chosen label-weight spaces. If the pairing separates P, they equal the simultaneous toral eigenspaces; without separation distinct labels may have the same toral character, so a spectral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space. Morphisms and the weight submodules/quotients considered on this page preserve this grading. Integrable means E_i and F_i are locally nilpotent on each vector. Finite dimensions and bounded support are additional hypotheses, not part of integrability. The zero module has the empty grading. Ordinary type-one modules for a separating datum recover the usual definition. Regularization of finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons are proved by the local realization supplier, not assumed by writing P=Hom(Pvee,Z).

For any characteristic-zero field k and q↦1, the positive toral quotient U_A^0⊗_A k/(K_h-1) is the polynomial algebra k[H_i], H_i=Tbar_{i,0,1}, with Tbar_{i,c,t}=binom(H_i+c,t). No residual K_h ambiguity remains AFTER this stated quotient; K_h need not equal1 in the unquotiented specialization. On any U_A-stable label-graded weight lattice M_A=⊕_mu(M_A∩M_mu), K_h specializes to the identity and T_{i,c,t} acts by binom(<mu,h_i>+c,t), even over Z for these scalar operators. The E/F/H_i operators satisfy the classical Cartan commutators. The lattice must actually have this grading; it is not inferred merely because it spans a weight module.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $\lambda\in P$. Let $U_q^{\ge0}:=U_q^0U_q^+$ be the subalgebra generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $E_i$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]) and let $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda$ be the one-dimensional $U_q^{\ge0}$-module with $K_h\cdot1=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}1$ and $E_i\cdot1=0$. The **quantum Verma module** is
$$M(\lambda):=U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda,$$
a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module ([[def-quotient-ring]] gives the quotient ring structure; the tensor product is over the subalgebra $U_q^{\ge0}$). Its image $v_\lambda:=1\otimes1$ is a **highest weight vector** of weight $\lambda$: $K_hv_\lambda=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v_\lambda$, $E_iv_\lambda=0$, and $M(\lambda)=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.

(i) $M(\lambda)$ is a weight module with $M(\lambda)_\mu\cong U_q^-[\lambda-\mu]$ as $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector spaces via $x\mapsto xv_\lambda$, where $U_q^-[\nu]$ denotes the root-graded component of degree $-\nu$; in particular $M(\lambda)$ is a free left $U_q^-$-module of rank one and every weight of $M(\lambda)$ lies in $\lambda-Q_+$.

(ii) **Universal property.** For every $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $V$ and every vector $v\in V$ with $K_hv=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v$ and $E_iv=0$ for all $i,h$, there is a unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $M(\lambda)\to V$ with $v_\lambda\mapsto v$; if $V=U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ then this map is surjective, and every quotient of $M(\lambda)$ generated by a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda$ arises this way.

(iii) **Simple quotient.** The sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper submodules of $M(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule (every proper submodule misses $v_\lambda$, because $v_\lambda$ generates $M(\lambda)$), and
$$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$$
is a simple $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, generated by the image of $v_\lambda$; it is the unique simple quotient of $M(\lambda)$, and every simple $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module generated by a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

The definitions of $N(\lambda)$ and $L(\lambda)$ use the sum of *all* proper submodules rather than a maximal submodule, so no choice principle is used. No claim is made here that $M(\lambda)$ has finite-dimensional weight spaces (its weight spaces $U_q^-[\nu]$ are finite-dimensional by [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i), but this is not part of the present definition), nor that $L(\lambda)$ is integrable: integrability is treated in [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]].
changed_native_views.current_statement: For lambda∈P, put M(lambda)=U_q⊗_{U_q^{≥0}}Q(q)_lambda, with E_i acting as0 and K_h asq^{<lambda,h>} on the inducing line. Give it the canonical P-label grading: via triangular decomposition, M(lambda)_{lambda-nu}=U_q^-[-nu]v_lambda. Its highest line is Q(q)v_lambda and every component is finite dimensional (there are finitely many words of a given height). A specified highest vector in a P-graded module gives the unique degree-preserving map from this Verma module; it is surjective for a cyclic highest module. The sum N(lambda) of all proper graded submodules is proper because each has zero top component; thus L(lambda)=M(lambda)/N(lambda) is the unique simple graded quotient. For separating torus data this is the usual simple weight-module quotient. The contravariant Cartan-projection lemma identifies N(lambda) exactly as a form radical and gives the canonical normalized form on L(lambda). Under dominance, the integrable theorem proves the ordinary simple and universal integrable conclusions. No arbitrary maximal submodule is selected.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and fix $i\in I$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]], [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). For every $P\in U_q^-$ there are unique $Q,R\in U_q^-$ with
$$E_iP-PE_i=\frac{K_iQ-K_i^{-1}R}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}.$$
Existence is the explicit computation that moves $E_i$ to the right through a word in the $F_j$: for $P=F_{j_1}\cdots F_{j_m}$ one has $E_iP-PE_i=\sum_{t:j_t=i}F_{j_1}\cdots F_{j_{t-1}}\frac{K_i-K_i^{-1}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}F_{j_{t+1}}\cdots F_{j_m}$, and moving each $K_i^{\pm1}$ to the left multiplies the remaining word by a power of $q_i$ (because $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_j$). Uniqueness follows from $K_iU_q^-\cap K_i^{-1}U_q^-=0$, which is the injectivity of the two maps $x\mapsto K_i^{\pm1}x$ and the linear independence of the toral components in the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]](i)-(ii)).

The **Kashiwara skew derivations** $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ are the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear maps
$$e_i'(P):=R,\qquad e_i''(P):=Q.$$
They are characterized by $e_i'(1)=e_i''(1)=0$, $e_i'(F_j)=e_i''(F_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and the twisted Leibniz rules: for homogeneous $x$ of root degree $\mathrm{wt}(x)\in Q$ and any $y\in U_q^-$,
$$e_i'(xy)=e_i'(x)y+q_i^{\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}xe_i'(y),\qquad e_i''(xy)=e_i''(x)y+q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}xe_i''(y);$$
equivalently, on left multiplication by generators,
$$e_i'F_j=q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_je_i'+\delta_{ij},\qquad e_i''F_j=q_i^{a_{ij}}F_je_i''+\delta_{ij}.$$
Both operators preserve the root grading and lower the root degree by $\alpha_i$: $e_i'(U_q^-[\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[\nu-\alpha_i]$ and similarly for $e_i''$, the target being understood as $0$ when $\nu-\alpha_i\notin Q_+$; in particular both operators are locally nilpotent on every homogeneous component of $U_q^-$, since the root degree has finite height. These operators are the negative-half case of the maps $\bar r_i,r_i$ of Lusztig's book and of $e_i',e_i''$ of the JKK paper; the definition above is the JKK one, and the two are related by the semilinear bar involution $\psi$ of $U_q^-$ (which fixes every $F_i$ and sends $q\mapsto q^{-1}$): $e_i''=\psi\,e_i'\,\psi$, since $\psi\,e_i'\,\psi$ has the same value $\delta_{ij}$ on each $F_j$ and the same twisted Leibniz rule with twist $q_i^{-\langle\mathrm{wt}(x),h_i\rangle}$. No choice principle is used.
changed_native_views.current_statement: For P∈U_q^- define e_i'(P)=R and e_i''(P)=Q by E_iP-PE_i=(K_iQ-K_i^-1R)/(q_i-q_i^-1), with Q,R∈U_q^-. The published triangular decomposition gives uniqueness of these two toral coefficients; moving E_i through generator words gives existence on the actual Serre quotient. The maps are Q(q)-linear, vanish on1, and send F_j to δ_ij. For actual weight wt(F_j)=-alpha_j, e_i'(xy)=e_i'(x)y+q_i^{<wt(x),h_i>}x e_i'(y) and e_i''(xy)=e_i''(x)y+q_i^{-<wt(x),h_i>}x e_i''(y). Thus e_i'F_j=q_i^{-a_ij}F_je_i'+δ_ij and e_i''F_j=q_i^{a_ij}F_je_i''+δ_ij. Writing the negative component as U_q^-[-nu] for nu∈Q_+, these maps take it to U_q^-[-(nu-alpha_i)] (zero when nu-alpha_i is not positive). They remove one letter, increase actual weight by alpha_i and decrease positive height by one, hence are locally nilpotent. They obey e_i''=psi e_i' psi under the bar. These are equivalently the corresponding primitive-leading-term coefficient maps of the braided half coproduct, with the same twists; the commutator construction fixes which coefficient is e_i' rather than e_i''. No imaginary-root convention is used.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its skew derivations $e_i'$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

A **Lusztig-Kashiwara form** on $U_q^-$ is a bilinear form $(\ ,\ ):U_q^-\times U_q^-\to\mathbb Q(q)$ satisfying
$$(1,1)=1,\qquad (F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))\quad\text{for all }i\in I,\ P,Q\in U_q^-.$$

The recursion determines at most one such form: it forces $(P,1)=\epsilon(P)$ for all $P$ (apply it to a decomposition $P=\sum_iF_iP_i$ of $P$ by first letters, with $e_i'(1)=0$, and iterate), hence $(1,Q)=\epsilon(Q)$ by symmetry, hence the value of $(P,Q)$ for every pair by induction on the total root degree of $P$, using again that every element of positive degree is a sum $\sum_iF_iP_i$ with the $P_i$ of strictly lower degree. Here $\epsilon$ is the counit, which on the root-graded half is the projection to $U_q^-[0]=\mathbb Q(q)\cdot1$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]).

Existence of a form satisfying the recursion (that is, well-definedness of the recursively computed value, which is the same as compatibility with the Serre relations defining $U_q^-$) is not part of this definition: it is the first assertion of [[thm-the-negative-half-bilinear-form-is-symmetric-nondegenerate-and-integral]]. The corresponding construction on the free algebra on the $F_i$ is the standard one of Lusztig's book, where the form is first defined on the free algebra and then descended by taking the quotient by its radical; the identification of that radical with the Serre ideal is where the substance of the existence statement lies. No choice principle is used in the uniqueness argument.
changed_native_views.current_statement: The normalized Lusztig-Kashiwara form is a homogeneous Q(q)-bilinear form B on U_q^- with B(1,1)=1, B(U_q^-[-nu],U_q^-[-mu])=0 for nu≠mu, and B(F_iP,Q)=B(P,e_i'Q). Equivalently the degree-zero normalization is B(1,Q)=epsilon(Q) together with the recursion. Homogeneity/counit normalization is essential: recursion and B(1,1)=1 alone do not force symmetry or uniqueness. The normalized form is unique by peeling first letters in the first argument. Its existence, symmetry and nondegeneracy are proved by the separation/form suppliers; the divided-power integrality normalization is specified in the form theorem, not assumed in this Definition.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $(\ ,\ )$ be the Lusztig-Kashiwara form on the negative half $U_q^-$ of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], with skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and $(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ exists on $U_q^-$, and every such form is symmetric; by the uniqueness in [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]] there is exactly one such form. (No separate right-adjunction formula for $(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: the symmetry is the source's statement, and in the rank-one subalgebra a formula $(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in (iv) show.)

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[\nu],U_q^-[\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\neq\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\neq x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with $(x,y)\neq0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the $A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then $W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and $(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is *not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here $[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Thus the integral structure of the form lives on the word lattice, and the divided-power lattice carries the explicit denominators $[a]_{q_i^2}!$. The form is nondegenerate on $W\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q^-$ but is not $A$-valued on $U_A^-$ in this normalization.
changed_native_views.current_statement:
Let $(\ ,\ )$ be the Lusztig-Kashiwara form on the negative half $U_q^-$ of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], with skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and $(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ exists on $U_q^-$, and every normalized homogeneous form satisfying these conditions is symmetric; by the uniqueness in [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]] there is exactly one such form. (iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the $A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then $W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and $(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is *not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\,\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here $[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Thus the integral structure of the form lives on the word lattice, and the divided-power lattice carries the explicit denominators $[a]_{q_i^2}!$. The form is nondegenerate on $W\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=U_q^-$ but is not $A$-valued on $U_A^-$ in this normalization. Globally, let A_loc=A[[r]_i!^{-1}:i∈I,r≥1], equivalently invert the Gaussian factorials [r]_{q_i^2}!, since their ratio is a Laurent unit. Then B(U_A^-,U_A^-)⊂A_loc: divided-power words are word vectors divided by finite products of these factorials. This is an exact denominator bound, not a false A-integrality assertion.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ be a dominant integral weight, put $m_i:=\lambda(h_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for $i\in I$, let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma module with highest vector $v_\lambda$ and $L(\lambda)$ its simple quotient ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]).

(i) **The integrable quotient.** $\tilde N(\lambda):=\sum_{i\in I}U_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$ is a proper submodule of $M(\lambda)$, and
$$\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\tilde N(\lambda)$$
is a nonzero highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ which is integrable: $\tilde L(\lambda)$ has a weight decomposition with weights in $\lambda-Q_+$, and both $E_i$ and $F_i$ act locally nilpotently on it.

(ii) **$L(\lambda)$ is integrable, and it is the unique simple integrable highest weight module of weight $\lambda$.** (a) Every integrable highest weight module $V$ of weight $\lambda$ has $F_i^{m_i+1}v=0$ for all $i$ on its highest weight vector, hence is a quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$. (b) Let $N(\lambda)$ be the sum of all proper submodules of $M(\lambda)$ ([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]). Since $\tilde N(\lambda)$ is a proper submodule, $\tilde N(\lambda)\subseteq N(\lambda)$, so $L(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$ is a quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$; hence $L(\lambda)$ is integrable as a quotient of an integrable module. (c) If $V$ is simple and integrable of highest weight $\lambda$, then $V$ is a simple quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$ by (a), and since every proper submodule of $M(\lambda)$ is contained in $N(\lambda)$ this forces $V\cong L(\lambda)$. (d) Conversely every simple quotient of $\tilde L(\lambda)$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$ as well, and $\tilde L(\lambda)$ is simple if and only if $L(\lambda)=\tilde L(\lambda)$; the last identity is established in [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]].

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]). Let $\sigma$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear anti-involution of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ defined on the generators by
$$\sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^{-1},\qquad \sigma(F_i)=q_i^{-1}K_iE_i,\qquad \sigma(K_h)=K_h .$$
(These assignments respect the defining relations, so $\sigma$ exists and $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$; it is the anti-involution of JKK (2.2).)

A bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$ on $L(\lambda)$ is **contravariant** if it is symmetric, $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$, and
$$(xu,v)=(u,\sigma(x)v)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U_q(\mathfrak g),\ u,v\in L(\lambda).$$
Equivalently (JKK (2.3)), it is the unique bilinear form with $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$ and
$$(q^hu,v)=(u,q^hv),\qquad (E_iu,v)=(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad (F_iu,v)=(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv)$$
for all $i,h,u,v$; the equivalence uses $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and the symmetry.

Then: the form exists and is unique (the recursion determines the value on $u$'s of increasing weight height starting from the highest weight vector); it is symmetric and nondegenerate; distinct weight spaces are orthogonal: $(L(\lambda)_\mu,L(\lambda)_\tau)=0$ for $\mu\neq\tau$; and nondegeneracy is equivalent to the non-vanishing of the determinant of the Gram matrix on each weight space. On a simple module the kernel $\{u:(u,L(\lambda))=0\}$ is a submodule not containing $v_\lambda$, hence is zero, which gives nondegeneracy once existence and symmetry are known. No choice principle is used; the source's convention for $K_i$ is $q_i^{h_i}$ with the torus inverted by $\sigma$, which is the library's convention ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).
changed_native_views.current_statement: Fix the Q(q)-linear anti-involution sigma with sigma(K_h)=K_h, sigma(E_i)=q_iF_iK_i^-1 and sigma(F_i)=q_i^-1K_iE_i (JKK(2.2)); it fixes q and is different from the semilinear contravariant tau. For lambda dominant and L(lambda) the normalized simple highest module, a contravariant form is a homogeneous symmetric bilinear form with B(v_lambda,v_lambda)=1 and B(xu,v)=B(u,sigma(x)v). Such a form exists uniquely, is nondegenerate on every finite label-weight space, and different label-weight spaces are orthogonal. Let $\lambda\in P^+$, let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$, and let $V_A:=U_Av_\lambda\subseteq L(\lambda)$ be the $A$-lattice generated by $v_\lambda$ under the integral form $U_A$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]].

(i) **Free integral weight lattices.** $V_A$ is stable under $U_A$ and $V_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)=L(\lambda)$; for every $\mu\in P$ the weight component $(V_A)_\mu=V_A\cap L(\lambda)_\mu$ is a finitely generated torsion-free (hence free) $A$-module, and $\mathrm{rank}_A(V_A)_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu<\infty$. In particular every weight space of $L(\lambda)$ is finite-dimensional.

(ii) **Specialization.** Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ made an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$ and put $\bar V:=V_A\otimes_Ak$. Then $\dim_k\bar V_\mu=\mathrm{rank}_A(V_A)_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$ for every $\mu$, and the action of $U_A$ on $\bar V$ factors through the specialization, so that $\bar V$ is a module over the specializations $\bar U_A^\pm$, $\bar U_A$ of [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]] and, through the half isomorphisms, over $U(\mathfrak n^-)_k$ and $U(\mathfrak n^+)_k$; it is an integrable module of highest weight $\lambda$ over the classical enveloping algebra (the action of $\bar T_{i,0,1}$ is the classical coroot action and $\bar E_i,\bar F_i$ are locally nilpotent because they are specializations of locally nilpotent operators with integral exponents).

(iii) **Character.** The weight multiplicities of $L(\lambda)$ equal those of the classical simple integrable highest weight module $L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$ of the Kac-Moody algebra $\mathfrak g$:
$$\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu=\dim_kL_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)_\mu\qquad(\mu\in P),$$
so $\mathrm{ch}L(\lambda)=\mathrm{ch}L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$ is given by the classical Weyl character formula. When the classical module is finite-dimensional (in particular for finite-type Cartan data) this also gives $L(\lambda)=\tilde L(\lambda)$, and the specialized lattice $\bar V$ has the character of $L_{\mathfrak g}(\lambda)$.

All freeness statements are over the principal ideal domain $A$; the hypothesis that $q$ is transcendental is used only through the nonvanishing of the $[m]_i$, and the coefficient field $k$ is required to contain $\mathbb Q$ so that the toral specialization $[K_i;c,t]\mapsto\binom{\mu(h_i)+c}{t}$ is defined. AC is inherited from [[prop-specialization-at-q-one-recovers-the-classical-enveloping-relations]].

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $M$ be an integrable weight module over $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$; write $F_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]]). Then:

(i) For every $\lambda\in P$ the weight space is the internal direct sum $$M_\lambda=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}\bigl(\operatorname{Ker} E_i\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\bigr).$$

(ii) Every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique expression $$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker} E_i\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$ with $u_n=0$ for all but finitely many $n$; this is the $i$-string decomposition of $u$.

(iii) For every $n\ge0$ and $\mu\in P$ the map $F_i^{(n)}:\operatorname{Ker} E_i\cap M_\mu\to M_{\mu-n\alpha_i}$ is injective when $\langle h_i,\mu\rangle\ge n$ and is the zero map when $\langle h_i,\mu\rangle<n$. Consequently in (ii) one has $F_i^{(n)}u_n\ne0$ whenever $u_n\ne0$, and $\operatorname{Ker} E_i\cap M_\mu=0$ whenever $\langle h_i,\mu\rangle<0$.

No finite-dimensionality of weight spaces, no boundedness of the weights and no uniform nilpotence exponents are assumed, and no choice principle is used; only local nilpotence of $E_i$ and $F_i$ enters.

Consequently M_lambda is the internal direct sum of these nonzero admissible string subspaces. changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $M$ be an integrable weight module and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ with $u_n\in\operatorname{Ker} E_i$ and $u_n=0$ for $n\gg0$. The **Kashiwara operators** are the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $M$ defined by $$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$ They have the following properties:

(a) $\operatorname{wt}(\tilde e_iu)=\operatorname{wt}(u)+\alpha_i$ if $\tilde e_iu\ne0$, and $\operatorname{wt}(\tilde f_iu)=\operatorname{wt}(u)-\alpha_i$ if $\tilde f_iu\ne0$; both operators preserve the weight decomposition, and $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ map weight vectors to weight vectors (or to $0$).

(b) $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker} E_i$. The linear map $p_0:M\to\operatorname{Ker} E_i$, $u\mapsto u_0$, is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker} E_i$ along $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n)}(\operatorname{Ker} E_i\cap M)$, and $$\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_M,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\operatorname{id}_M-p_0 .$$ In particular $\tilde f_i$ is injective, $\tilde e_i$ is surjective and $(1-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i)M=\operatorname{Ker} E_i$.

(c) (naturality) If $\varphi:M\to N$ is a homomorphism of integrable $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules, then $\varphi\tilde e_i=\tilde e_i\varphi$ and $\varphi\tilde f_i=\tilde f_i\varphi$.

(d) (agreement with the classical operators) $\tilde f_iu=F_iu$ for every $u\in\operatorname{Ker} E_i$, and $\tilde e_iu=E_iu$ for every $u$ with $F_iu=0$. The operators are not the classical generators globally: in the three-dimensional simple $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module with highest weight vector $v_2=F_i^{(0)}v_2$ and $u=F_i^{(1)}v_2$ one has $F_iu=0$ but $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v_2\ne0$.

No choice principle is used.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Let $A_0$ be the local ring of [[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]] and let $M$ be an integrable weight module with its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]], [[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]).

A **crystal lattice** of $M$ is a free $A_0$-submodule $L\subseteq M$ such that (i) $L$ generates $M$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, i.e. $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L\to M$ is an isomorphism; (ii) $L=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}L_\mu$ with $L_\mu:=L\cap M_\mu$; (iii) $\tilde e_iL\subseteq L$ and $\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$ for all $i\in I$. Because $A_0$ is a principal ideal domain, a free $A_0$-submodule of a weight piece $M_\mu$ has a well-defined rank, and (ii) says that the rank of $L$ is the sum of the ranks of the $L_\mu$.

A **crystal basis** of $M$ is a pair $(L,B)$ consisting of a crystal lattice $L$ and a $\mathbb Q$-basis $B$ of the crystal limit $L/qL\cong\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L$ ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]) such that
(iv) $B=\bigsqcup_{\mu\in P}B_\mu$, where $B_\mu:=B\cap(L_\mu/qL_\mu)$;
(v) $\tilde e_iB\subseteq B\cup\{0\}$ and $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B$ for all $i\in I$;
(vi) for all $b,b'\in B$ and all $i$: $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$; here $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ denote the operators induced on $L/qL$.
The axiom $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B\cup\{0\}$ is stated for completeness; in fact $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B$ automatically, because $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}$ implies that $\tilde f_i$ maps no nonzero class to $0$.

The **crystal graph** of $(L,B)$ is the coloured directed graph with vertex set $B$ and an arrow $b\xrightarrow{i}b'$ whenever $\tilde f_ib=b'$ (by (vi) this is equivalent to $b=\tilde e_ib'$). The **crystal of $M$** is this graph, together with the weight function $b\mapsto\mu$ for $b\in B_\mu$. For every $\mu\in P$ one has $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu=\#B_\mu$: the first equality holds because $L\otimes_{A_0}\mathbb Q(q)\cong M$ respects the weight decomposition by (ii), and the second because $B_\mu$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L_\mu/qL_\mu$.

A **crystal basis of the negative half** $U_q^-$ is defined by the same data with $U_q^-$ in place of $M$: a free $A_0$-submodule $L\subseteq U_q^-$ with $U_q^-\cong\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L$ and $\tilde e_iL,\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), together with a $\mathbb Q$-basis $B$ of $L/qL$ satisfying (v) and (vi) for the operators on the negative half. Here the root grading replaces the weight grading, and no weight decomposition axiom is needed because $U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ is already graded. No choice principle is used in these definitions.

Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable weight module $M$ as in [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], and let $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ be the induced operators on $L/qL$.

(a) For $b\in B_\mu$ define $\operatorname{wt}(b):=\mu\in P$; this is well defined because the $B_\mu$ are disjoint, and $K_h$ acts on any lift of $b$ by the scalar $q^{\langle h,\mu\rangle}$.

(b) For $i\in I$ and $b\in B$ define $$\varepsilon_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde e_i^{\,n}b\ne0\},\qquad \varphi_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde f_i^{\,n}b\ne0\}.$$ Both are finite: $\varepsilon_i(b)$ is finite because the weights $\operatorname{wt}(b)+n\alpha_i$ of $\tilde e_i^{\,n}b$ are distinct and lie in the weight set of $M$, and $\varphi_i(b)$ is finite because the weights $\operatorname{wt}(b)-n\alpha_i$ are distinct and $\tilde f_i^{\,n}b\ne0$ would exhibit infinitely many distinct weights; alternatively, for lifts in a finite portion of the module, the string decomposition bounds both lengths.

(c) The **$\varepsilon$-$\varphi$ relation**: for every $b\in B$ and $i\in I$, $$\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\operatorname{wt}(b)\rangle .$$ This is the rank-one statement that the $i$-string through $b$ is the crystal of a simple $U_{q_i}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module of highest weight $\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\operatorname{wt}(b)\rangle\ge0$, whose length is that highest weight plus one.

(d) **Arrows.** For $b\in B$ and $i\in I$: $\varepsilon_i(b)\ge1$ if and only if $\tilde e_ib\ne0$, if and only if there is $b'\in B$ with $b=\tilde f_ib'$; and $\varphi_i(b)\ge1$ if and only if $\tilde f_ib\ne0$, if and only if there is $b''\in B$ with $b=\tilde e_ib''$. Moreover, for $b\in B$ with $\tilde e_ib\ne0$ (respectively $\tilde f_ib\ne0$): $$\operatorname{wt}(\tilde e_ib)=\operatorname{wt}(b)+\alpha_i,\quad \varepsilon_i(\tilde e_ib)=\varepsilon_i(b)-1,\quad \varphi_i(\tilde e_ib)=\varphi_i(b)+1,$$ $$\operatorname{wt}(\tilde f_ib)=\operatorname{wt}(b)-\alpha_i,\quad \varepsilon_i(\tilde f_ib)=\varepsilon_i(b)+1,\quad \varphi_i(\tilde f_ib)=\varphi_i(b)-1 .$$

(e) The **crystal graph** is the coloured graph with vertex set $B$ and arrows $b\xrightarrow{i}\tilde f_ib$; (c) and (d) say that every $i$-string is a finite chain $$b_{\text{top}}\xrightarrow{i}b_{\text{top}-1}\xrightarrow{i}\cdots\xrightarrow{i}b_{\text{bot}},$$ of length $\varepsilon_i+\varphi_i+1$, with $\varepsilon_i$ counting the arrows above $b$ and $\varphi_i$ those below. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); in this page we write $V(\lambda):=L(\lambda)$, following the notation of the crystal sources. Define $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $V(\lambda)$ generated by all vectors $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ ($r\ge0$, $i_1,\dots,i_r\in I$), where for $r=0$ the vector is $v_\lambda$; and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $U_q^-$ generated by all $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1$ ($r\ge0$), where $\mathbf 1$ is the unit of $U_q^-$. Define
$$\mathcal B(\lambda):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda+q\mathcal L(\lambda)\ :\ r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda),$$
$$\mathcal B(\infty):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1+q\mathcal L(\infty)\ :\ r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty).$$

Then, with $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$, the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear surjection with $\pi_\lambda(\mathbf 1)=v_\lambda$:

(a) $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$ with $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}=\mathcal L(\infty)\cap U_q^-[-\nu]$; correspondingly $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)=\bigsqcup_\nu\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\nu}$.

(b) $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$, $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$; $\pi_\lambda(\mathcal L(\infty))\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\pi_\lambda$ maps the generating monomials of $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to those of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$.

(c) (recursive spanning) For $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, $$\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\sum_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i},\qquad \mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}\Bigr)\setminus\{0\},$$ and the same formulas with $\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$. Each $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ and each $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is generated over $A_0$ by finitely many monomials of total length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$, hence is a finitely generated $A_0$-module.

No freeness, no basis property and no crystal-lattice property of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ or $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is asserted here; these are the conclusions of [[thm-grand-loop-existence-of-highest-weight-crystal-bases]] and [[thm-crystal-basis-of-the-negative-half]]. The script letters avoid the collision with the simple module $L(\lambda)$: Kashiwara and JKK write $L(\lambda),B(\lambda),L(\infty),B(\infty)$ for these lattices and bases. No choice principle is used.

(a) **String decompositions.** $v_2=v_2$ (the $n=0$ component is $v_2$), $v_1=F_1^{(1)}v_2$ (component $u_1=v_2$), $v_0=F_1^{(2)}v_2$ (component $u_2=v_2$). Hence
$$\tilde e_1v_2=0,\quad \tilde e_1v_1=v_2,\quad \tilde e_1v_0=v_1,\qquad \tilde f_1v_2=v_1,\quad \tilde f_1v_1=v_0,\quad \tilde f_1v_0=0 .$$
In particular $F_1v_1=[2]_1v_0\ne0$ while $\tilde f_1v_1=v_0$, and $F_1v_0=0$ while $\tilde f_1v_0=0$: the Kashiwara operator $\tilde f_1$ agrees with $F_1$ on $\operatorname{Ker} E_1=\mathbb Q(q)v_2$ but not on the interior of the string, and $\tilde e_1$ agrees with $E_1$ on lowest weight vectors.

(b) **Crystal.** $\mathcal L(2\omega)=A_0v_2\oplus A_0v_1\oplus A_0v_0$ is a crystal lattice of $V$, and $\mathcal B(2\omega)=\{b_2,b_1,b_0\}$ with $b_2=v_2+q\mathcal L(2\omega)$, $b_1=v_1+q\mathcal L(2\omega)$, $b_0=v_0+q\mathcal L(2\omega)$ is a crystal basis with crystal graph $b_2\xrightarrow{1}b_1\xrightarrow{1}b_0$. (c) **Partial inverses.** $\tilde e_1\tilde f_1=\operatorname{id}_V-p_{\mathrm{bot}}$ and $\tilde f_1\tilde e_1=\operatorname{id}_V-p_0$ where $p_0$ is the projection $v_2\mapsto v_2$, $v_1,v_0\mapsto0$ onto $\operatorname{Ker} E_1$; evaluated at $v_2$ this shows the failure at the top of the string: $\tilde f_1\tilde e_1v_2=0\ne v_2$. **Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There are $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s\in P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j=1}^sV(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used exactly once, to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects bases of the finite-dimensional maximal-vector spaces simultaneously. Given that decomposition, all lattice and crystal arguments below are choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Fix $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ and the crystal limiting ring $A_0\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ of [[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]], and put $A_\infty:=\psi(A_0)$, the image of $A_0$ under the semilinear involution $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, i.e. the ring of rational functions regular at $q=\infty$; $A_0$ and $A_\infty$ are the two charts of $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Z}$ over which the globalization is performed.

Let $M$ be one of $U_q^-$ or $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ ($\lambda\in P^+$). Equip $M$ with the bar involution $\psi$ of [[lem-the-lusztig-integral-form-is-stable-under-bar-and-contravariant-duality]]: on $U_q^-$ the semilinear algebra involution $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$; on $V(\lambda)$ the induced semilinear involution determined by $Pv_\lambda\mapsto\psi(P)v_\lambda$ (well defined because the highest vector is fixed). Let $M_A\subseteq M$ be the divided-power integral form: $M_A=U_A^-$ for $M=U_q^-$, and $M_A=V_A(\lambda):=U_A^-v_\lambda$ for $M=V(\lambda)$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]; $U_A^-$ and $V_A(\lambda)$ are $\psi$-stable). Let $L$ be the Kashiwara crystal lattice of $M$ over $A_0$: $L=L(\infty)$ for $U_q^-$ and $L=L(\lambda)$ for $V(\lambda)$ ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]], [[thm-grand-loop-existence-of-highest-weight-crystal-bases]]).

Define the **bar lattice** $L^-:=\psi(L)$, an $A_\infty$-submodule of $M$, and the **balanced part** $E:=M_A\cap L\cap L^-$. The definition keeps three structures on the same $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space strictly separate: the $A$-module $M_A$, which is not assumed free and not claimed to be contained in $L$; the free $A_0$-module $L$; and the free $A_\infty$-module $L^-$. No equality $L^-=L$, no inclusion $M_A\subseteq L$, no freeness of $M_A$ and no identification $E=M_A$ are asserted; those are conclusions of the balanced-triple construction. changed_native_views.original_statement: Fix a partition lambda and a residue i. The uncancelled opening brackets are the good (or normal) addable i-nodes, and the uncancelled closing brackets are the cogood (or conormal) removable i-nodes; the leftmost uncancelled opening bracket is the good node and the rightmost uncancelled closing bracket is the cogood node. The good node is the unique addable i-node minimizing N^r_i and the cogood node is the unique removable i-node minimizing N^l_i; moreover a partition is i-regular at the good node in the following sense: the addable i-node selected at q=0 is exactly the one whose addition keeps the e-regularity of the connected component.

changed_native_views.original_statement:
Fix $e\ge2$ and let $\Lambda_0$, $\alpha_i$ and $Q$ be the level-one data of the cyclic affine type $A_{e-1}^{(1)}$ Cartan datum of [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]. This page works in the following fixed convention, called the *symmetric-group convention*, and every later item of the pair refers to it.

(i) *Residues and nodes.* Diagrams are English, rows increase downwards, and nodes are written $(r,c)$. The residue of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod e\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$, and a node is an *$i$-node* if $c-r\equiv i$; the $i$-nodes of a partition are its addable and removable $i$-nodes ([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]). This is the residue convention of the level-one partition Fock space ([[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]]) and of the modular signature ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). It is the negative of Brundan's residue $r-c$; by Brundan's Remark 2.4(II) his normal rows of $\lambda$ are exactly the rows $i$ for which the node $(\lambda_i,i)$ is a Kleshchev-normal node of the transpose $\lambda'$, and the two conventions must never be mixed silently.

(ii) *The two label classes.* A partition $\lambda$ is *$e$-regular* if no non-zero part of $\lambda$ occurs $e$ times, and *$e$-restricted* if $\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}<e$ for all $a\ge1$ (equivalently: no $e$ equal column heights, i.e. $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular). Conjugation $\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) interchanges the two classes. For $e=0$, Kleshchev's convention for the case where no non-trivial $e$-th root of unity exists, both conditions are vacuous and every partition is both $e$-regular and $e$-restricted.

(iii) *Crystal labels versus simple labels.* The vertex labels of the level-one crystal on this page are the $e$-restricted partitions, read with the modular signature of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] (i-nodes from top to bottom, cancellation of a $-$ above a $+$, good $=$ topmost normal, cogood $=$ bottommost conormal). The simple-module labels are the $e$-regular partitions, tied to the crystal labels by the transpose/sign dictionary $D^{\mu}\cong D(\mu^{t})\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ of [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].

(iv) *Conjugation dictionary.* The map $(r,c)\mapsto(c,r)$ is a bijection from the nodes of $\lambda$ onto the nodes of $\lambda'$, sends addable nodes to addable nodes and removable nodes to removable nodes, and satisfies $\operatorname{res}(c,r)=-\operatorname{res}(r,c)$. It therefore matches the $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ with the $(-i)$-nodes of $\lambda'$ as sets, and interchanges the $e$-restricted and $e$-regular strata. It reverses the top-to-bottom and the column orders of nodes.

(v) *Weight.* The weight function used throughout is $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i$, where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of $i$-nodes of $\lambda$. Under conjugation $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda')=\Lambda_0-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_{-i}$, i.e. the diagram automorphism $i\mapsto-i$ is applied to the weight; no weight is identified with $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda)$ without it.

Work in the convention of [[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]] and let $A\ne B$ be addable or removable nodes of one residue $i$ of a partition $\lambda$.

(i) If $A$ is strictly above $B$ ($\operatorname{row}(A)<\operatorname{row}(B)$), then $A$ is strictly to the right of $B$ ($\operatorname{col}(A)>\operatorname{col}(B)$). In particular no two addable or removable $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ share a row or a column, the top-to-bottom order of the $i$-nodes is exactly their order of decreasing columns, and the content $c-r$ increases strictly along the top-to-bottom order. Hence the content order of [[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]] (larger content $=$ further right) is the top-to-bottom order, and the order of increasing columns is its reverse.

(ii) Consequently the $i$-signature read from top to bottom is the reverse of the $i$-signature read by increasing columns; cancelling a $-$ above a $+$ in the first reading is the mirror image of cancelling a $+$ before a $-$ in the second, and the two reductions have the same set of surviving nodes, with the leftmost surviving $-$ of the first reading equal to the last surviving $-$ of the second, and the rightmost surviving $+$ of the first equal to the first surviving $+$ of the second.

(iii) Conjugation $\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ restricts to a bijection from the $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ onto the $(-i)$-nodes of $\lambda'$ that preserves addability and removability and reverses the reading orders: the top-to-bottom order of the $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ corresponds to the increasing-column order of the $(-i)$-nodes of $\lambda'$.

(iv) Consequently the modular rule of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] applied to $\lambda$ at residue $i$ and the Fock rule of [[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]], read on the column-decreasing order of $\lambda'$ at residue $-i$, have the same reduced words, the same surviving nodes and the same good and cogood extrema.
